title: Why You Shouldn't Pep-Talk Difficult Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2013/09/21/why-you-shouldnt-pep-talk-difficult-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues against the common practice of pulling difficult students aside for encouraging pep-talks, contending it can worsen behavior rather than improve it. He explains that most difficult students have heard endless pep-talks before and have grown jaded to them, that talks lacking a basis in real improvement carry no meaning, and that visible teacher desperation for change hands students leverage they can exploit. He also argues that frequent individual attention reinforces a damaging label of being 'different' rather than capable. Instead, he recommends restrained, small gestures of acknowledgment—like eye contact or a fist bump—reserved for moments of genuine, self-driven improvement.
points: Frequent pep-talks with difficult students can worsen behavior rather than improve it, contrary to common intuition.
Most difficult students have heard so many pep-talks over the years that they've become jaded and adept at tuning them out or telling teachers what they want to hear.
Visible teacher desperation for a student's improvement hands that student leverage they can exploit to disrupt the classroom.
Frequent individualized attention can reinforce the damaging belief that a student is fundamentally 'different' rather than simply a student who has misbehaved.
Recommended alternatives are small, restrained, and private acknowledgments—eye contact, a nod, a fist bump—reserved for genuine, self-driven improvement.
quotes: The student stands wordlessly, eyes averted, still smarting from yet another backslide as the earnest teacher softens the blows of the student’s many transgressions.
But pulling difficult students aside for pep-talks, particularly in response to recent misbehavior, will not only delay real and lasting improvement, but it can cause behavior to worsen.

Most difficult students have a history of misbehavior reaching as far back as preschool. Add the near-constant flow of pep-talks over the years, and you have a group of students who have heard it all.
When difficult students see how desperate you are for them to improve, you hand over much of the leverage you need to help them change their ways.

Eye contact and a nod from across the room, a knowing smile and a fist bump, a note folded over and waiting on their desk . . . these authentic moments between you mean the world to students labeled as “difficult.
